newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - MG bounces back with 70 pct profit hike.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - MG bounces back with 70 pct profit hike.

text.p: Germany's Metallgesellschaft AG (MG), the diversified engineering and trading group rescued from the brink of bankruptcy in 1994, on Monday reported a 70 percent jump in pre-tax profits in 1995/96.

MG went on to say that the higher earnings trend would be maintained in the current year. "No precise forecast can yet be made for the fiscal year. However we expect to beat the previous year's result," management board chairman Kajo Neukirchen said.
Speaking at the company's annual results news conference, Neukirchen said pre-tax profit in the year to September 30 rose to 292 million marks from 171 million marks.
Neukirchen said its financial situation had improved in 1995/1996, with its equity capital ratio rising to 6.7 percent from 2.2 percent and bank debt falling further.
MG said its medium-term target for rate of return on capital employed is 14 percent and that it was confident this value orientation would be rewarded by investors.
Neukirchen did not give a date for when MG would resume dividend payments, which it stopped paying three years ago.
Group sales fell to 15.8 billion marks from 17.6 billion.
"Most of the decline in sales was planned and is the result of the rapid implementation of our strategy."

"The chief contributory factors were the sale of the lead smelters, the disposal of peripheral activities in the trade subgroup and the winding down of oil and natural gas trading in the United States," said Neukirchen.

Looking to the current year, MG said it had a successful start in the 1996/1997 business year, with pre-tax profit in the first quarter to December 31 rising 20 percent to 26.7 million marks and sales up at 3.8 billion marks from 3.4 billion.
The 20 percent rise in group pre-tax profit in the first quarter of 1996/1997 cannot be extrapolated into a full-year forecast, Neukirchen said.
All MG's subsidiaries made a positive contribution to profits in 1995/1996 said MG, which has undergone a restructuring involving the sale of subsidiaries.

Neukirchen said an exact forecast was impossible because of MG may face substantial changes in its portfolio of shareholdings following the planned purchase of a 49.99 percent stake in industrial holding company AGIV.

One area given close attention was MG's operations in the United States, represented through MG Corp, where MG suffered nearly-crippling losses on oil futures deals in the early 1990s. The U.S. unit had fully unwound all of the contracts at the end of 1995.
The group's U.S. unit MG Corp represents only about three percent of the group's overall revenues of 15.8 billion marks.
All of the losses from the speculative oil trading were placed in MG Corp's U.S. accounts, where the unrealised profit had to be written down.
On October 1, MG sold is banking unit Metallbank to the private bank SchmidtBank for an undisclosed sum.

"In doing so we have reacted promptly to the process of concentration in the banking market and the disadvantaging of banks owned by conglomerates by the amending law to the Banking Law (KWG)," said Neukirchen.

Last Friday MG said it was seeking a settlement with its disgraced former chairman Heinz Schimmelbusch and its former finance director Meinhard Forster, saying it planned no severance pay for Schimmelbusch.
MG said the ex-chairman, who has been blamed for leading MG to the brink of bankruptcy in late 1993, and Forster, had accepted clear responsibility for financial problems created at the group.
